बॉलीवु़ड में बेबाक अंदाज दिखाना प्रकाश राज को पड़ गया भारी! 🎬

पत्नी पोनी वर्मा ने एक इंटरव्यू में बताया कि राजनीतिक विचारों के कारण प्रकाश राज के हाथ से कई फिल्में और ad प्रोजेक्ट्स निकल गए। 💔

पोनी के मुताबिक, साल 2017 में करीबी दोस्त गौरी लंकेश की हत्या के बाद प्रकाश अंदर से टूट गए थे और उन्होंने चुप रहने से मना कर दिया था। 🥀

पोनी का दावा है कि कई मेकर्स ने एडवांस देने के बाद भी फिल्मों से प्रकाश को हटा दिया और उन्हें Telugu इंडस्ट्री में कई बार बैन भी किया गया। 🚫

NEET पेपर लीक के बाद दिल्ली में CJP यानी Cockroach Janta Party के प्रदर्शन में भी प्रकाश शामिल हुए थे, जिसके बाद उन्होंने CEC Gyanesh Kumar के इस्तीफे की मांग की थी। 📢

शनिवार को भी प्रकाश ने लोकतंत्र बचाने के लिए दिल्ली में प्रदर्शन में शामिल होने की अपील का एक video शेयर किया था। ✊

वर्कफ्रंट की बात करें तो अजय देवगन की फिल्म Drishyam: The Conclusion में नजर आए प्रकाश राज जल्द ही SS Rajamouli की Varanasi और G2 में दिखने वाले हैं। 🎥

क्या कलाकारों को अपने राजनीतिक विचार खुलकर रखने चाहिए? 💬

ctx.title: Prakash Raj’s wife Pony Varma says actor lost films and ad deals over his political views
ctx.summary: Pony Verma says husband and actor Prakash Raj has suffered professionally for standing by his beliefs, losing film and advertising opportunities.
ctx.text:
Prakash Raj is among the few actors who openly express their political views. The actor was an active supporter and participant in the Cockroach Janta Party's (CJP) protest in Delhi following the NEET paper leak. In a recent interaction, his wife, Pony Verma, spoke about how Prakash has lost work because of his outspoken political views.
Speaking to Prema The Journalist, Pony recalled how Prakash was "devastated completely and broken" after his close friend and journalist Gauri Lankesh was shot dead in 2017. She shared that Gauri's death shook him and that he refused to remain silent, deciding instead to raise pertinent questions. However, she also admitted that Prakash's outspoken nature has often cost him work.
She said the actor lost several film opportunities and advertising assignments because of his political positions. "We all know Prakash is a fearless man. He was banned in Telugu multiple times. He stands his ground. He will believe in certain things and do it with 100% conviction. Several films, people have simply backed off after paying advance."
She added, "I know how much his work got affected in the industry. The way the ads went off, films were taken away from him. He has suffered immensely in his profession. But he says, my conscience says what is happening is wrong, so I should not accept this.”
Pony also recalled the time Prakash participated in the CJP protest in Delhi and how ‘shaken and scared’ she was during the Chalo Sansad march after witnessing lathi charges and pellets guns used against protestors. However, she said Prakash remained unfazed. He told her that at least the mothers of the protesting students would know that he was standing alongside their children.
After the NEET protest, Prakash joined the CJP movement, which demanded the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar and opposed the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls. He also spoke out against the detention of CJP leaders.
On Saturday, Prakash shared a video urging people to join a protest in Delhi, calling for collective action to protect democracy. “Please join us in Delhi tomorrow for protest to save our democracy,” he said. The appeal comes amid concerns over electoral transparency and democratic rights, with protesters questioning the electoral process.
On film front, Prakash was last seen in Ajay Devgn's blockbuster Drishyam: The Conclusion. He has SS Rajamouli's Varanasi and Vinay Kumar Sirigineedi's G2 in pipeline.

She began her career covering Delhi's cultural scene, food, nightlife, concerts, and city life at The Times of India, before moving into full-time entertainment journalism with India Today.

At India Today, Vibha interviewed some of the biggest names in Bollywood and television while carving a niche for herself through film reviews, opinion pieces, nostalgic features, celebrity interviews, and trend-driven stories. She later brought her storytelling and editorial expertise to The Indian Express, where she continued to deepen her understanding of cinema through long-form entertainment explainers, retrospectives and feature writing.
